articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress following resignation
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress following resignation
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down as CEO of the chipmaker he co-founded 33 years ago and built into a $4 trillion company that powered the artificial intelligence boom, the company announced Thursday.
CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," said board chair Harvey Jones in a release announcing the news.
The company will begin the search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang and will consider both internal and external candidates, according to the release.
Kress also provided a statement in the release, but Huang was not quoted.
After a meteoric rise to fame due to Nvidia's central role in AI, Huang's dramatic fall has been even more rapid, following a series of stinging revelations about his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy.
Huang, 63, apologized on Sunday for being "unfaithful to my wife," though he provided no details about the affair with businesswoman Alice Huang, who has worked for a Chinese company and Nvidia customer called Megaspeed. Late Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the Nvidia CEO also had a separate affair, this one with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at the chipmaker. Later that afternoon, The Times and other outlets reported that Nvidia's board met to discuss the company's future.
Huang's downfall also puts the spotlight on President Donald Trump , who formed a particularly close relationship with the CEO of what, until recently, was the world's most valuable company. Huang became a key voice on U.S. AI policy while pushing for issues that were in Nvidia's interest, such as preserving access to open-source AI, and lobbying to allow chip exports to China.
Nvidia's board decided last night to oust longtime CEO Jensen Huang, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said sentiment quickly turned after the report of a second alleged affair.
The team worked late into the night on its communications strategy and made an official decision this morning, before naming Kress as interim CEO, the person added.
— Seema Mody, Samantha Subin
Super Micro Computer shares fell 12% after Bloomberg reported that the U.S. Justice Department is looking into whether organizations associated with Alice Huang, the woman suspected to be a Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia's Jensen Huang, were involved in diverting Super Micro's artificial intelligence hardware to China.
In March,  U.S. prosecutors charged three people who had been connected with Super Micro, including co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw, with smuggling billions worth of Nvidia-powered servers into China. Liaw and the other two are no longer affiliated with the company, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York, which originally made the allegations about the smuggling, is leading the investigation, according to Bloomberg , which cited one unnamed person in its report
University of Colorado Law professor Ann Lipton, a corporate law and governance expert, said that following Huang's resignation, the Nvidia board will need to "move swiftly" to present a succession plan, which will be difficult given Huang's centrality to the business.
The board should also "make clear to investors that it is on top of the situation" and how it is filling holes left in Huang's absence.
The CEO's resignation, Lipton said in an e-mail, "demonstrates the seriousness of the underlying allegations, and will strengthen any shareholder claims regarding damages, the importance of any misrepresentations, and Huang's likely knowledge of the truth. "
Following reports that Huang had an affair with a purported Chinese spy, Rosen Law Firm in New York filed a proposed class action lawsuit on behalf of investors who saw the value of their Nvidia stock decline rapidly.
Rosen Law attorney Phillip Kim told CNBC in an e-mail that investor interest in joining the class action has been high. "It's a widely held stock," he wrote. In just a few days, he added, "several hundreds of investors" had contacted his firm, ranging "from mom and pops to investors with very large losses."
Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top-ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Trump's reported reaction to troubling U.S. intelligence about Huang demands scrutiny.
"All the reports say that Trump knew what took place and just basically made it like it was no big deal," Meeks said when asked if Trump was too trusting of Huang, his close ally.
"Those are the things that have to be looked at," Meeks said.
When asked if Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick or Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler should be called to testify, Meeks said, "Look, I think that anybody that could answer some questions, anybody that might have been involved."
"If it's up to me, I'm going to at least have some questions or some hearings. The American people need to know," he added.
— Kevin Breuninger and Justin Papp
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said Huang's departure does not obviate the need for him and Nvidia to answer to Congress.
"Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer wrote in an X post.
"The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset," Schumer wrote.
"Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump's relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One? Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships," the Senate leader wrote.
Democratic leaders on the Senate Finance Committee and House Ways and Means Committee are launching an investigation into the Trump administration's approval for the export of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to Chinese government-linked companies.
Their letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announcing the probe was sent by Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Rep. Richard Neal, D-Mass., the respective ranking members of the Senate and House committees.
Wyden and Neal noted that, despite Trump's reported knowledge of U.S. intelligence showing Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy, his administration "did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat."
"On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang's compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales," the letter read.
They described a "scheme" in which Trump would let Nvidia sell Taiwanese H200 chips to Chinese companies, provided they undergo a security review in the U.S. and receive an export license, subjecting them to 25% U.S. tariffs.
"The Trump Administration's ostensible attempt to mask an unconstitutional export tax as a national security tariff action — benefitting both Nvidia and the Chinese government — raises serious concerns within our Committees' jurisdiction over matters relating to taxation and tariffs," they wrote.
Jensen Huang's $140 billion Nvidia stake is largely held by trusts that are co-owned with his wife, Lori, according to SEC filings.
The arrangement further complicates Huang's sudden exit from the company, but could prove to be a stabilizing force for the shares, since the trusts make it more difficult for either Huang or his wife to quickly sell, lawyers told CNBC.
Here is why ultra-rich founders use these trusts and how they could work in the event of a divorce.

articles.title_orig: While many Americans resist, China embraces AI data center boom
articles.title_zh: While many Americans resist, China embraces AI data center boom
articles.content_orig:
Ulanqab, China — Off a major highway on the outskirts of Ulanqab, in the Chinese province of Inner Mongolia, Hereford cows roam through corn fields scouring the ground for any dried up remains of the recent harvest.
Hovering over the landscape are shiny new transmission towers linked by power cables that stretch along the plateau for as far as the eye can see. On the ridgeline, covered in snow, wind turbines spin, taking full advantage of the ever-blowing wind.
The energy pulsing from the remote Chinese region — a combination of renewables and fossil fuels — will soon power multi-story data centers being constructed on farmland as part of a sprawling AI data center construction boom .
The construction site is the size of a small American city. It is the biggest, and fastest growing infrastructure project anywhere in China right now.
This corner of Inner Mongolia was famous for generations for growing potatoes. Now, it's fast becoming an AI hub, and Chinese officials hope the expansive, rugged landscape will help power the country's ambition to surpass the U.S. as the global leader in artificial intelligence.
Baletu, a 72-year-old farmer, who has lived here for more than 40 years growing potatoes and corn, said the changes across his local landscape are positive.
"It doesn't affect my farmland, not at all," he told CBS News. "It's good for the area."
A short drive away, CBS News was able to see what all that wind power will soon be feeding. Trucks, cranes and thousands of workers are taking part in the construction project to create one of the biggest data centers anywhere in the world.
We drove miles down new roads with multistory data centers going up on either side. Even from the road it was easy to spot the countless racks that will hold servers, semi-conductor chips and cooling and exhaust fans.
There are dozens of data centers being built in Inner Mongolia, more than any other part of the vast nation. The reason they have chosen Ulanqab is because it offers cheap, abundant energy. Fossil fuels are still the main source of power here, but they also use renewables, including wind and solar.
Ulanqab is one of the most consistently windy locations in the province. The climate is also cold all year, which helps keep cooling costs down, and land and labor are more affordable in the remote region.
Experts cited by the Financial Times say data centers in China are built at about one-fifth of the costs incurred in the U.S., not least due to the much higher land and labor costs.
As many as 30,000 workers have been brought in from across China to help build the AI hub, and in a country experiencing an economic downturn and high youth unemployment, these mass infrastructure projects are very much welcome.
"Development is the best thing, especially when it provides job opportunities for many young people," a local businesswoman who sets up a lunchtime food stall outside the construction site told CBS News.
While data centers in the U.S. face major community opposition , which could be emboldened by the "blue wave" of the Democrats' stunning midterm election performance, there are few hurdles for Chinese developers.
While China's government doesn't generally tolerate protests of any kind, and it tightly controls messaging across all media, a United Nations survey last year found that as many as 80% of people in the country support data center construction. At least two-thirds of Chinese people use AI in their day-to-day life, as many embrace the technology and the infrastructure behind it.
Under President Xi Jinping, AI development has become a national strategic priority for China .
"There is no opposition to data centers in China. It's never heard of, whereas in the U.S., it has become a huge movement against data center building in neighborhoods," Henry Wang, founder and president of the Center For China and Globalization, told CBS News.
Huawei, Alibaba, Byte Dance, Deepseek, Baidu, Z.ai, ZData and VNET — China's biggest AI companies — are all active in Inner Mongolia. In areas where construction has finished, fences are up and grounds are landscaped, and avenues through the humming data centers have been named after the AI tech giants.
While Chinese firms' AI models are believed to be about six months behind their U.S. competitors, due largely to restrictions on the sale of high-end microchips, the gap is narrowing.
China has more than double the power generation capacity of the U.S., and some experts believe access to power, not chips, will ultimately be the deciding factor in the global race for AI dominance.
"Chips may not become the latest diving criteria," said Wang. "It may be that power is the bottleneck, and whoever goes through that first gets the advantage. And right now. China has the edge."

Russian news agencies are reporting further comments from US envoy Steve Witkoff after his meeting with Putin earlier today.
Witkoff reportedly said a new round of trilateral talks with Russia and Ukraine had been agreed , with Europeans also set to join the meeting.
I’ll bring you the full quotes as soon as we have them.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today .
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are on their way to Dublin to meet with Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy ( 18:04 ) after their talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier today ( 14:16 , 14:41 , 17:28 , 17:49 ).
During the meeting, the leaders discussed Russia’s key demands when it comes to the peace process and agreed to hold another round of talks on Ukraine war, reportedly adding Europeans to the table ( 16:59 ).
But during the meeting Putin struck a notably tough tone repeating many of his maximalist demands that are unlikely to be acceptable to Ukraine or Europe ( 15:24 ).
Separately, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy warned against “strange” attempts agree on “a new security framework between Europe and Russia,” and urged European leaders to “pay attention” to what is being proposed ( 13:04 ).
He also revealed that Starshield systems, which play a critical role for Ukraine’s army, appeared to be throttled again, disrupting its ability to defend itself from Russian attacks ( 10:08 , 13:07 ).

Speaking to CNN and Russian media on departure from Moscow, Witkoff said :
“ I think progress was made today. … I think it was made earlier today. Abu Dhabi was, people didn’t think that we were going to restart trilateral. We’ve restarted it; we’ve set a new meeting now on top of that, and this is what President Trump wants to see.”
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have left Moscow en route for Dublin where they are going to meet with Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ireland’s public broadcaster RTÉ reported.
Flightradar24 records show that they are now in fact in Helsinki, Finland and they are expected to continue the trip to Ireland shortly.
Your guess is as good as mine as to whether they are in the Finnish capital just to refuel their plane or perhaps they are catching up with Finland’s influential president Alexander Stubb , who play an important role in the peace process behind the scenes.
The Kremlin said that talks between Russian president Vladimir Putin ⁠and two ⁠US envoys ​had been useful and that the American ⁠side had supported Putin’s proposal for a joint humanitarian ⁠mission to a city ​in eastern Ukraine, Reuters reported.
Yuri ‌Ushakov, the ‌Kremlin aide, said Putin would ‌continue discussions on Ukraine with US president Donald Trump at an A pec summit in China later this month and ‌that direct peace talks with Ukraine, which resumed this ​week after a pause of 9 months, would continue.
Ushakov said that Russia had made ⁠clear to the US envoys that ​ Nato ​could not expand ​further and expressed hope ​that Europe ‌would support ​talks ​on a new European security architecture.
A controversial bill approved in October in the lower house of Italy’s parliament includes measures that allow healthcare workers who were struck off their professional registers during the pandemic for serious violations connected to their anti-vaccination beliefs – for example, promoting treatments that lacked a scientific basis – to apply to be reinstated.
The bill is being championed by the prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party and is strongly backed by its far-right coalition partner, the League.
But with allies in Forza Italia split, its approval in the lower house hinged on support from National Future (FN) , a rival far-right force led by the former army general Roberto Vannacci , whose emergence is shaping the political landscape before general elections next year. Vannacci has voiced opposition to vaccine mandates, and his rhetoric frequently targets the vaccine-sceptic audience.
The measure still needs to clear the senate, with a vote scheduled in January. But its progress has alarmed medical experts, less because of the number of healthcare workers involved – it is believed to be very small – and more because of the risk of further eroding trust in vaccines.
Nearly one in two Italian adults are hesitant about vaccination, according to a report by the department of public health and paediatric sciences at the University of Turin published in the Lancet Regional Health Europe in February. The report, which sampled 50,000 adults across Italy, found the ambivalence was driven more by misinformation and lack of institutional trust than by fears over vaccine safety.
Here’s the full quote from Witkoff, via Reuters:
“The Europeans will join at the next meeting, which we consider to be a very important moment ⁠because they are our partners and it’s important to us that they take part.”

Meanwhile, a London-based naval drone maker founded by Ukrainians has reached a £4.5bn valuation after it raised more than £500m from investors including the UK government.
UForce, which makes military drones for land, air and sea, received £113m from the UK’s national wealth fund. The investment makes UForce one of the UK’s fastest-growing unicorns – or startups with a valuation of more than $1bn. Its drones have been used extensively in the war in Ukraine .
The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, met the UForce chief executive, Oleg Rogynskyy, on Thursday onboard the British aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales during a defence conference in Oslo, Norway.
The UK’s Ministry of Defence noted UForce’s maritime capabilities in particular, amid concerns over the increasing threat from Russia in the north Atlantic and North Sea. Russian naval vessels and its “shadow fleet” have been accused of sabotage and spying operations on cables and pipelines , while the UK is planning a fleet of sea-borne drones in the northern seas to track Russia’s nuclear submarine fleet .
Streeting on Thursday piloted a UForce MV7 uncrewed vessel located more than 1,500 miles away in the Atlantic Ocean near Portugal.

Prosecutors said Georgescu managed an organised crime group that prompted ⁠a Romanian businessman to give them €1.1m by making him believe they could help ⁠him get a credit line of up to €15m ​from a foreign ‌financial institution, Reuters reported.
Georgescu has ‌been in pretrial detention since late September. In posts ‌on Georgescu’s Facebook account, his wife, Cristela Georgescu, denied the charges and said they were politically motivated.
Vladimir Putin’s comments during his meeting with the two US envoys make it clear that getting a deal with Russia will not be easy.
During his talks with Witkoff and Kushner, the Russian president doubled down on his demand to retain the Russia-occupied Ukrainian territory and opposed any foreign peacekeeping troops in the country – a key part of Europe’s planned security guarantees for Kyiv.
Instead, he continues to push for broader talks on rolling back Europe’s post-1997 Nato security architecture, a move which Zelenskyy called “strange” and urged Europe to watch closely.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: US FDA shelves commissioner's voucher program for speedy drug reviews, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: US FDA shelves commissioner's voucher program for speedy drug reviews, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The FDA has quietly shelved the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher (CNPV) pilot program, a controversial speedy review process launched by former agency head Marty Makary, M.D., Reuters reports , citing six sources familiar with the matter, as well as internal documents.
Meanwhile, the FDA also appears to have paused publishing complete response letters after briefly halting—and then resuming—the practice in July.
The CNPV was designed to accelerate reviews for drugs and companies that support U.S. national interests, such as meeting large unmet medical needs and onshoring of development and manufacturing. The ultra-accelerated process shortens the FDA’s review from the regular 10 months to just one to two months.
The pilot’s rollout since June 2025 has been controversial, as public concerns run the gamut from political favoritism and lack of transparency to straining the FDA’s bandwidth. So far, 22 drug programs have received the voucher, with 12 approvals and one rejection to date.
The reported pause doesn’t appear to be permanent. In a statement to Fierce, an HHS spokesperson said work under the CNPV is “ongoing.” At least for programs that have already received a CNPV, the FDA is committed to executing on the promised timeline.
“FDA career staff continue to evaluate applications granted a CNPV, meet commitments for accelerated review and enhanced engagement, and assess best practices emerging from the pilot program,” the spokesperson said.
The FDA is still accepting applications for CNPV but is not reviewing or granting new ones, Reuters reported, citing one person familiar with the process. The most recent CNPV grants appear to be for a trio of psychedelics in April following an executive order from President Donald Trump, and one disclosed in May for Partner Therapeutics’ cholangiocarcinoma drug Bizengri. There’s no public record of any new CNPVs following Makary’s resignation as the FDA commissioner in mid-May.
The council of FDA leadership responsible for making critical decisions around CNPV has gone dormant, Reuters asserted, citing internal documents. The FDA’s recent review documents for Revolution Medicines’ pancreatic cancer drug Rasonque, which was among the cohort of nine programs that got the initial batch of CNPVs, do not show any involvement of the council. Instead, the review was conducted and decided by the Oncology Center of Excellence under the pre-existing real-time oncology review framework.
Controversy over the program flared up in May when Sanofi reportedly asked that its diabetes drug Tzield be withdrawn from the CNPV track after then-director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, Tracy Beth Høeg, M.D., Ph.D., tried to overturn staff’s recommendation for approval.
After a leadership overhaul, the FDA in June held a public hearing about CNPV. While existing CNPV beneficiaries voiced support for the program by highlighting a sense of collaboration, they also offered suggestions for improvement, such as clearer feedback from the review council.
The medical and academic communities were more critical. Peter Lurie, M.D., a former FDA employee and current president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, called for the agency to shut down the pilot due to concerns about “politicization in voucher selection and review, strained agency resources and lack of transparency.”
In a statement to Fierce Thursday, the HHS spokesperson said: “FDA will continue advancing reforms aimed at improving efficiency, accelerating scientific review, strengthening public trust, and delivering measurable results for patients, families, and consumers.”
The legality of the CNPV program has also drawn scrutiny. In a February letter (PDF) to Makary, Rep. Jake Auchincloss, a Democratic congressman from the biotech hub that is Massachusetts, suggested that the agency does not have statutory authority to establish CNPV, and he targeted the political nature of the review council.
“My investigation has revealed an FDA replete with conflicts of interest, illegal maneuvers, and political interference,” Auchincloss wrote in the letter.
CNPV isn’t the only initiative launched by Makary that has faced legal pushbacks. Last summer, touting “radical transparency,” the FDA started publishing all complete response letters in a public database in real-time. However, in a Citizen Petition filed in April, the law firm Covington & Burling argued that the practice could be violating federal laws meant to protect confidential information.
As the FDA has included a legislative proposal in its fiscal year 2027 budget request, asking Congress to grant it clear statutory authority to publicly disclose information related to CRLs, the agency appears to have put new releases on hold.
No new entries have been logged into the FDA’s CRL database for the past three months. The most recent one was a manufacturing-related rejection for ITM Isotopes Technologies’ radiopharmaceutical candidate ITM-11 in early August.
Following the legal challenge and after a three-month hiatus, the FDA had initially confirmed to Fierce in July that it had halted the release of those rejection letters. But then the agency released a new batch of CRLs and told Fierce that it plans to publish more “appropriately redacted” CRLs.
In response to Fierce’s questions about CRL disclosure policy Thursday, an FDA spokesperson said: “Transparency and public confidence are central to the FDA's mission. The FDA remains committed to the proactive release of Complete Response Letters and will continue to publish appropriately redacted CRLs.”

articles.title_orig: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.title_zh: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: 2 children among the 8 dead in New York City building collapse, officials say
An Israeli airstrike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight killed at least six people, the Health Ministry in the Palestinian enclave said Thursday.
The strike hit a surgery building at Nasser Hospital, with medical staff and patients among those killed, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, health officials said. The Israeli military said it was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants.
The strike — the latest despite an ongoing U.S.-backed ceasefire — shattered ceilings and left debris strewn across wards inside the hospital, which is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza after the destruction of Israel’s yearslong military assault.
Palestinian surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira was among those killed, the Health Ministry said. He was featured in the 2026 documentary “American Doctor,” which followed three American doctors helping to provide medical care in Gaza.
Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid, head of the surgery department at Nasser Hospital, said there was no “notice, warning or anything” before the hospital was attacked. “Suddenly, there was fire and shelling and walls were brought down instantly,” he said.
He said he was not aware of any “resistance fighters or combatants present — only a medical team treating patients.”
NBC News also spoke with two surgeons who said they were in the hospital when the missile struck after traveling to Gaza from the U.K. earlier this month to assist with medical care.
Both Dr. Goher Rahbour, a consultant general and colorectal surgeon, and Dr. Stephan Verborg, a limb reconstruction surgeon, said they were also not aware of any warning from the Israeli military before the strike, which hit the hospital shortly after midnight.
“I heard the impact and I felt the explosion because the whole hospital shook,” Verborg said in a phone interview Thursday. He said he was about 15 to 20 meters away from the point of impact, adding: “You could smell the smoke. You could see the dust.”
Rahbour said he had been operating with Abu Shaira, whom he described as a “lovely” and “affable” person, earlier that day. He said they had been laughing and joking together Wednesday evening in the hours just before the Palestinian surgeon was killed.
Both doctors had traveled to Gaza early this month through the organization IDEALS, a U.K. charity seeking to provide sustainable humanitarian aid to regions affected by conflict or natural disasters. They said they had not seen any indication of a Hamas presence in the hospital.
Tributes were paid to Abu Shaira. “Dr. Rizq was at the hospital during the entire war,” Dr. Mohammed Zaqout, director general of the Health Ministry in Gaza, could be seen telling a crowd of mourners, surrounding a body covered in a shroud, in a video captured for NBC News on Thursday. “He didn’t abandon his duties for even one day.”
Nasser Hospital said a 13-year-old boy, identified as Jihad Naeem Muhammad Abu Tilikh, was also among those killed.
The Israeli military and the Israel Security Agency said they struck a senior Hamas member, along with other militants, who they said had “advanced” attacks from the hospital in the southern Gaza Strip overnight. In a later statement, they identified the senior member as Muhammad Abu Ismail, who they said served as the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade and had also been responsible for holding hostages in Gaza.
The IDF and ISA said Hamas had “established a presence within the hospital complex and used it as a command center” and stored weapons and conducted interrogations and torture from within the medical complex. They shared photos of weapons alleged to have been found within the complex.
The IDF and ISA said steps had been taken to “mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.” They also later said “advance warnings were issued to the population.” The IDF said it was looking into reports that medical workers,  including Abu Shaira, and patients were killed.
One woman, Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza, said her brother, Khaled Abu Anza, was killed in the strike, with Nasser Hospital separately confirming his death.
A number of media outlets, including Israeli media outlet Ynet , reported that a commander in Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade of that same name was killed in the strike. Asked to confirm that and whether he was directly targeted, the IDF said it would get back on the matter.
Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza did not directly identify her brother, 53, as a Hamas member, but said she believed he was targeted. He had been at the hospital for physical therapy after undergoing surgery, she said.
“He did not come to the hospital to engage in combat or resistance. He came for medical treatment,” she said.
Hamas condemned the allegations that it was using the hospital for military operations as “lies of the criminal enemy” and called the attack a “war crime.”
Hospitals have protected status under international law, but they have been heavily targeted under Israel’s yearslong offensive in Gaza. The Israeli military has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating within medical facilities, a charge the militant group has denied.
The overnight attack was not the first time that Nasser Hospital itself has been targeted.
In August 2025, the hospital was hit by a double tap Israeli strik e that killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. The deadly attack sparked international outrage.
Of Gaza’s 37 hospitals, just two are considered to be “fully functioning,” while 18 are partially functioning and 17 are considered nonfunctioning after much of the enclave’s healthcare system was devastated under Israel’s offensive, according to data published by the World Health Organization.
Israeli strikes have continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement reached in October of last year.
More than 1,600 people have been killed since the truce came into effect, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry in the enclave. Israel says four of its ⁠soldiers have ​been killed in that time.
Both Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.
More than 74,600 people, including thousands of children, have been killed overall in Gaza since Israel launched its offensive in the enclave following the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, in which some 1,200 people were killed and around 250 taken hostage.
In a statement, Medical Aid for Palestinians, which supports several departments at Nasser Hospital, said the overnight attack was “yet another indication that the so-called ‘ceasefire’ has brought neither safety nor an end to Israel’s attacks on Gaza’s healthcare system.”
The latest strikes come as Palestinians contend with heavy rains and desperate conditions in the enclave as the colder months set in, prompting a fresh wave of outcry over the lack of progress in advancing the peace deal between Israel and Hamas.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: ‘Screwed twice’: The CFPB says it’s looking out for consumers. Its own data tells a different story
articles.title_zh: ‘Screwed twice’: The CFPB says it’s looking out for consumers. Its own data tells a different story
articles.content_orig:
Complaints about banks and other financial players keep rising as Trump officials squelch enforcement actions at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
This story was supported and co-published by the journalism
non-profit the Economic Hardship Reporting Project
Early in Donald Trump’s second term, his administration began ditching consumer protection lawsuits involving some of the nation’s biggest-name corporate players – including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway empire.
Under the command of Trump officials, the federal agency that had filed the suits – the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) – was signaling it no longer believed these companies were hurting everyday Americans.
Many consumers across the nation disagree.
As the CFPB abandoned these enforcement efforts, its own data began to tell a troubling story. In the year following the dismissals of the lawsuits, complaints against the vast majority of companies whose cases were dismissed increased – sometimes dramatically.
A Guardian analysis of CFPB data shows that across all banks and corporations named as defendants in the now-dropped suits, the number of complaints published to the agency’s public database shot up by more than 75%.
Of the 23 financial firms named as defendants, 17 saw increases in the number of complaints against them.
Complaints published to the CFPB database against Rocket Mortgage increased more than 130% in the year after the bureau dropped a lawsuit accusing its sibling company, Rocket Homes, of using kickbacks to steer borrowers to Rocket Mortgage.
Complaints against Branch Messenger Inc, which had been accused of working with Walmart to harvest more than $10m in unfair banking fees from the big box chain’s delivery drivers, shot up 315% in the year after the case was dismissed.
These increases are part of a larger trend of everyday Americans letting the CFPB know they have concerns about the way companies have treated them. Publicly posted complaints to the agency have grown from nearly 2.7m in 2024 to 6.3m so far this year.
Experts – and current and former CFPB employees – say the spike in complaints against companies freed from enforcement actions points to a disconnect between the bureau’s mission and its actions.
“Consumers are telling the bureau that there is an emergency, and the bureau is not listening or acting on that information,” said Erie Meyer, a former chief technologist at the CFPB who helped oversee the creation of its complaint database. “People are getting screwed twice: first by the company, second by the agency that’s supposed to stick up for them.”
The dismissals of enforcement actions are part of a wide-ranging campaign by the Trump administration to deplete or dismantle an agency created a decade and a half ago to counter the reckless and predatory practices that helped spawn the Great Recession.
Between mid-2012 and early 2025, the bureau publicly launched nearly 400 enforcement actions against banks and other financial firms – an average of roughly 30 a year, according to the agency’s website . These actions, the agency has previously said, helped provide aggrieved consumers with more than $21bn in restitution and canceled debts.
Since Trump’s inauguration on 20 January 2025, the CFPB has launched just two public enforcement actions, its website indicates – one announced several days later and another brought in August 2025.
The current leadership of the CFPB did not reply to a detailed list of questions for this story. Instead, an agency spokesperson claimed in a statement that the CFPB had cost Americans hundreds of billions of dollars – “making the American Dream, like homeownership, more costly by the thousands for each borrower”.
“This Weaponized agency attacked political enemies and disfavored industries and used novel legal theories and secret justifications to ruin lives and businesses,” the statement added. “We are fixing that and bringing the agency back to operating within statute and away from breaking the law and helping all business and Americans who were victims of thuggery.”
The Guardian’s reporting on the CFPB’s enforcement rollback came amid midterm elections that were in large part a referendum on the high prices Americans pay for gas, food and shelter. Last week’s results produced big wins for Democrats who lashed Trump for policies that fueled the rise in living costs.
The next battles over high prices and abusive business tactics may turn on how aggressive the midterms’ winners are in fighting to protect struggling consumers.
The White House did not reply to questions for this story.
When Amanda and Jason Riffle got married in 2024, they struggled to find a place for their blended family of five. Rents around Clarksburg, West Virginia, were too high for the amount of space they needed, Amanda Riffle said.
After Jason’s family gave them a plot of land as a wedding gift, the couple went shopping for a doublewide manufactured home. They found what they wanted – a four-bedroom, 2.5-bath Southern Charm model. It was sold and financed by two companies that are part of Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway conglomerate: Clayton Homes and Vanderbilt Mortgage & Finance.
Like many Americans who have sued, filed CFPB complaints or simply regretted their dealings with financial firms, the Riffles say that what they hoped to be a good thing for them turned out to be something else. In their case, they alleged in a lawsuit that Clayton and Vanderbilt sold them the doublewide using “bait-and-switch” tactics that raised their costs beyond what they had been promised.
The 2025 suit, filed in state court and later shifted to federal court, claimed the couple was promised that the price for the doublewide would be just over $250,000 – with installation costs included – but just before closing Vanderbilt increased the price to more than $290,000. They later learned that the market value of the Southern Charm model was between $180,000 and $200,000, according to the suit, which was settled on confidential terms.
“They show you one number, and then it changes,” Amanda Riffle said in an interview with the Guardian. “They really did rush us through everything: ‘You just need to sign here, you need to sign here.’ They did not go over those things in detail.”
Their lawsuit was filed just over three months after the CFPB walked away from its own lawsuit against Vanderbilt. The agency’s case, filed in federal court in Tennessee, alleged that Vanderbilt had made large numbers of loans on manufactured homes “without making a reasonable and good-faith determination that the borrowers could repay them”.
The CFPB’s claims were echoed by two other private lawsuits filed in federal court in West Virginia around the same time by Mountain State Justice, the non-profit legal aid group that handled the Riffles’ case.
Both of these lawsuits alleged Vanderbilt failed to realistically evaluate the affordability of the loans for financially unsophisticated borrowers.
One of these cases, which was also settled on confidential terms, alleges that the supposedly independent closing agent who helped oversee the signing of the documents on the plaintiffs’ loan was a former longtime salesperson for Clayton Homes who falsely claimed that he was the mayor of a small West Virginia town, using an email address that included the moniker “THE MAYOR41”.
The other case, which is set to go to trial in December, claims that one of the borrowers was “handicapped and reads at only a kindergarten level”.
CFPB data reviewed by the Guardian shows that the number of consumer complaints filed against Vanderbilt increased by 39% from the year before the CFPB dropped the case to the year after – rising from 84 to 117 complaints over that time.
In a statement, Vanderbilt said it “originates more than 20,000 loans and services more than 165,000 loans each year. The number of CFPB customer complaints we receive is extremely low, and a change of 33 c

articles.title_orig: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress Has Tried to Tame Nvidia’s Riskiest Bets
articles.title_zh: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress Has Tried to Tame Nvidia’s Riskiest Bets
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.
The influential co-founder of the AI chip-making giant resigned on Thursday over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress is in charge, for now, as the tech giant faces one of its biggest challenges - finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies.
We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.
Colette Kress has been an industry veteran for more than 30 years, having previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.
Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice-president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.
She has "fronted every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.
But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.
Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority.
Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology.
Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job.
Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications.
"He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.
Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.
Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced.
Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.
Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts.
Liu said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair.
Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant.
Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung.
Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana.
"The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said.
Ten Cap's Liu had believed it was just a matter of time before Huang would step down as Nvidia's chief executive.
"The issue is no longer simply about personal conduct," she said. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence in the leadership of one of the world's most strategically important companies."
Several major investment firms have downgraded their forecasts for the chip giant - a rare shift given investors' longstanding optimism about the company.
An early indication came as markets opened in New York shortly after Huang's resignation was announced.
Nvidia shares opened down more than 13%, wiping more than half a trillion dollars off the firm's share market value.
Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here".
Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines."
Ray Wang, chief executive of Constellation Research, said the crisis isn't so much an issue for the wider AI industry but rather one for Nvidia itself which has to consider if the person it appoints as its chief executive has the same appeal as Huang.
"That's really what the issue is, because a lot of these partnerships and investments have been made because of the trust with with Jensen," he said.
Additional reporting by Kali Hays

SpaceX is counting down to make history with the launch of its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13 , with liftoff scheduled for 5:45 p.m. EDT (2245 GMT) at Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land both Starship Ship and Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever full recovery of an orbital rocket and spacecraft, if successful.
Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which will also deliver 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.

STARBASE, Texas — We are one day until launch of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15, and Space.com is onsite here in Texas prepping cameras and coverage.
Liftoff is currently targeted for tomorrow (Nov. 13), during a 75-minute window opening at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT).
This flight could be a historic one for SpaceX and the space industry. For the first time, SpaceX will attempt to catch both stages of its massive Starship rocket — Super Heavy just minutes after launch, and the Ship upper stage roughly 22 hours later, following several orbits around Earth.
I'll be covering the action from here in Texas, so stay tuned to Space.com for updates as we count down to liftoff!
Happy Wednesday, Space Fans. We are now T-2 days away from SpaceX's planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 test mission, so I wanted to take a moment to give you a run down on what to expect.
Today, you can read my full guide to SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch here , which goes over what time and where to watch the launch online. Flight 15 will mark the first time SpaceX will attempt to land and catch both the Super Heavy booster (which it has done several times) and the Ship from orbit.
If successful, it will be the first full recovery of an entire orbital rocket from space.
Hello, Space Fans, and welcome to our coverage of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight , the first ever to attempt twin landings of the Starship Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage.
SpaceX has officially set the launch date for Flight 15 for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EDT (2145 GMT) . That puts launch just about 3 days away and Space.com will provide live coverage of the potentially historic flight, the first full recovery of an orbital rocket.
Space.com Spaceflight Writer Josh Dinner will be reporting live from near SpaceX's Starbase , Texas site for the launch, with myself (Tariq Malik), Spaceflight and Tech Editor Mike Wall and other team members tracking the flight remotely for you here. articles.title_orig: Megaspeed, chip firm at center of Nvidia scandal, pledges to cooperate with U.S. investigation
articles.title_zh: Megaspeed, chip firm at center of Nvidia scandal, pledges to cooperate with U.S. investigation
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: 2 children among the 8 dead in New York City building collapse, officials say
HONG KONG — Megaspeed, the tech company at the center of the Chinese spy scandal that engulfed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , said Thursday it will cooperate with the U.S. government’s investigations into the matter.
Megaspeed’s statement came hours before the resignation of Huang, one of the leaders of the AI boom, who co-founded the American chipmaker and helped build it into the world’s second most valuable company.
In its first statement since reports emerged about Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the future of the tech giant, Megaspeed said that it takes its obligation to comply with U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.”
U.S. intelligence agencies determined that Alice Huang had an affair with the Nvidia CEO and was a Chinese intelligence operative, a person with knowledge of the matter told NBC News on Sunday.
She held a senior position at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed is under U.S. criminal investigation for allegedly smuggling American-made chips into China in defiance of U.S. export controls.
A criminal investigation is ongoing in Singapore, where officials said Thursday Alice Huang had been barred from re-entering the country. The government also issued her with a stern warning after finding that she had knowingly provided police with inaccurate information to downplay her role in the company. It said that Huang was not investigated for espionage.
The country’s Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement that authorities had interviewed Huang and impounded her passport in 2025, but that its requests for cooperation from U.S. authorities had gone unanswered.
“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” it said.
Investigators concluded in February that there was “insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences,” the statement said, adding that investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals were continuing, related to the shipment of servers via Singapore.
Megaspeed, meanwhile, said in the statement Thursday that it has “cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority.” The statement was signed by its chairman and CEO, Tan Yong Pong, who also goes by James Tan.
It said that “Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government.”
China has dismissed the spying allegations as “smears.” On Thursday, a Foreign Ministry spokesperson said that “the U.S. side should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives as a pretext for implementing technological blockades.”
Megaspeed did not address the allegations surrounding Alice Huang, but said that “to further reinforce our commitment to compliance, Megaspeed has retained a leading U.S. law firm to lead a comprehensive census of its graphics processing units (GPUs) and independently verify its export control compliance practices.”
The company added that it “welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws.”
Nvidia’s stock price has plunged since its 63-year-old chief admitted over the weekend to being “unfaithful” to his wife.
Huang quit on Thursday in the wake of reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships. In a statement, Nvidia named its executive vice president and chief financial officer Colette Kress as its interim CEO.
Nvidia’s board met Wednesday night to address Huang’s future at the company, a source familiar with the matter told NBC News, adding that the White House was aware of the meeting.
The scandal has raised questions about how much U.S. government officials knew about Alice Huang and Megaspeed.
In the spring, Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a memo to officials in the Trump administration outlining how U.S. intelligence showed that the Nvidia CEO was in a romantic relationship with a business executive who was an asset of China’s spy service, according to a person familiar with Nvidia and a former national security official with knowledge of the matter. The New York Times and the Financial Times first reported on this memo.
Alice Huang’s precise role and relationship with China’s spy service remain unclear, however. It’s possible she was not a career spy for China’s spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, but was asked to cooperate and share information based on her access to Huang, a former national security official with knowledge of the matter told NBC News.
Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., ranking Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, told NPR that Alice Huang’s role still needed to be clarified.
Democrats will soon hold control of both the House and the Senate and, as a result, will have subpoena power.
On Wednesday night, as the Nvidia board met, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Coons, D-Del., announced they had written to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick with a request to preserve records on the subject.
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.

President Donald Trump suggested Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace Jensen Huang as the head of Nvidia following Huang's abrupt resignation amid scrutiny of his personal conduct and potential national security concerns.
"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The president's endorsement comes as Nvidia faces a leadership shake-up following Huang's departure from the artificial intelligence chipmaker he co-founded in 1993.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial on Sept. 2, 2026, in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images)
Cook stepped down as Apple's CEO in September after 15 years at the helm and now serves as the iPhone maker's executive chairman. Trump did not indicate whether Cook had expressed interest in taking the helm at Nvidia.
Huang's resignation followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.
The allegations raised questions about whether the longtime technology executive could have been targeted by Chinese intelligence, given Nvidia's central role in the global artificial intelligence industry and ongoing U.S.-China tensions over advanced chips.
No evidence has been publicly established that Huang disclosed confidential information or that the woman obtained Nvidia secrets. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto)
The reported relationship has fueled concerns about potential foreign intelligence efforts to gain access to sensitive information involving one of America's most strategically important technology companies. However, no evidence has been publicly established that Huang disclosed confidential information or that the woman obtained Nvidia secrets.

articles.content_orig:
Joe is based in Brussels, where he focuses on European politics and defence. He has covered the Ukraine war and its peace negotiations and reported on US elections from Washington DC
Britain and France should immediately deploy troops to Ukraine, a former head of Nato has said.
Anders Fogh Rasmussen accused Europe’s two nuclear powers of presiding over a “coalition of the waiting” while the Kremlin dragged out peace talks.
“For some months, France and the UK have tried to establish a coalition of the willing, but it’s more now a coalition of the waiting,” the 73-year-old former Danish prime minister told The Telegraph from his office in Brussels.
“We should transform that into a ‘coalition of the doing’ by deploying troops… you could not wait for a peace deal but actually push for peace by telling Putin ‘you cannot deter us, and we will help the Ukrainians defend against attacks against their critical infrastructure’.”
Mr Rasmussen’s call for action came during US-led negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine and Russia, which focused on security guarantees and preventing a future war.
European officials were kept out of the room after Moscow objected to their involvement in the two-day talks, which Ukraine described on Wednesday as “one of the toughest” negotiations yet.
Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, said after the talks: “We have no idea what the Europeans are doing here, this is a trilateral meeting. They can hang out in the lobby if they want.”
Mr Rasmussen, who was Nato’s secretary-general between 2009 and 2014, believes that Europe must show Vladimir Putin that it is serious in its support for Ukraine, even as it continues to be denied a seat at the table.
He has devised a five-point strategy to stop the war and prevent Europe from “sleepwalking into a permanent war on the Continent”.
He called on Germany, Spain and Greece to empty their stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to help Kyiv protect itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks, and suggested Nato extends its integrated air and missile defence systems over western Ukraine to bolster defences.
On top of this, Mr Rasmussen said the EU should confiscate more than €200bn (£175bn) in frozen Russian assets and use them to top up Kyiv’s defence budget. The “Coalition of the Willing” should be overhauled to include only countries willing to go to war with Russia should it attack Ukraine after any ceasefire is negotiated, he added.
“President Trump has chosen Moscow and sided with Vladimir Putin,” Mr Rasmussen said. “So in Europe, we have a particular responsibility for helping Ukraine, and that’s why I call on European leaders to wake up.”
He added: “It’s clear that the Russians do not want peace. Putin has no incentives to engage in the peace negotiations as long as he believes he can succeed on the battlefield.
“So, we need to change his calculus, we need to put more pressure on Russia.”
His plan would involve French and British troops as a “reassurance force” to protect Ukraine’s population centres.
It would also free up more Ukrainian resources to commit to the front line with Russia.
Mr Rasmussen insisted that such a deployment would be in line with international rules as long as it was requested by Kyiv.
However, Mr Rasmussen’s ideas are likely to be controversial amongst Europe’s Nato allies.
Numerous countries have said they would not actively shoot down Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory for fear of becoming a genuine party to the conflict.
Belgium has repeatedly blocked EU discussions about using a tranche of frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine’s defence.
While Germany has recently warned that it cannot donate any more Patriot interceptor missiles because it doesn’t have the stockpiles to defend its own country.
“Maybe Poland is in a different situation, but Germany, I don’t understand why they cannot deliver those Patriot systems. Deliver them now; they are needed right now in Ukraine… Germany is not threatened now,” Mr Rasmussen said.
The former Nato chief, who was involved in talks with Russia when it first invaded Ukraine’s Crimea peninsula in 2014, said the Continent was right to reopen communication channels with Moscow.
But he warned against linking discussions on a ceasefire in Ukraine to negotiations over a future European security architecture, arguing that Putin would seek to exploit the talks to restrict the military capabilities of both Kyiv and the alliance.
That said, Mr Rasmussen believes Nato could ultimately offer Russia security guarantees, given that its allies have no plans to attack Moscow.
“Why not? It wouldn’t cost anything to give such a security guarantee,” he concluded.

articles.title_orig: Israeli Strikes on Gaza Hospital Kill 6 and Injure Dozens, Health Officials Say
articles.title_zh: Israeli Strikes on Gaza Hospital Kill 6 and Injure Dozens, Health Officials Say
articles.content_orig:
The Israeli military struck a hospital in the southern Gaza Strip on Thursday, killing at least six people and injuring 28 more, according to local health officials.
Dr. Ahmed al-Farra, general director of Nasser Hospital, said in a news conference on Thursday that two missiles had hit the facility and that among the dead was Rezeq Abu Shaira, 52, a doctor.
Health officials reached in Gaza by phone said that a man called Khaled Abu Anza had also been killed. A spokeswoman for the Israeli military, speaking on condition of anonymity in line with protocol, said that Mr. Abu Anza was a Hamas operative.
The Israeli security agency and military said in a joint statement on Thursday that they had targeted Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom they identified as a Hamas commander “responsible for holding numerous hostages captive” during the Gaza war.
The Israeli authorities said that Hamas had established a command center at the hospital complex to stage operations against Israeli forces and was storing weapons there. They added that steps had been taken to mitigate harm to civilians.
Hamas said the Israeli claim that the hospital was used for military activity was a “blatant attempt to justify a heinous crime targeting a civilian medical facility.” Residents of Gaza have said that officials affiliated with Hamas-run Gaza government and security forces sometimes use the enclave’s hospitals as offices.

articles.title_orig: Nintendo Reveals Switch 2 Black Friday Deals (US)
articles.title_zh: Nintendo Reveals Switch 2 Black Friday Deals (US)
articles.content_orig:
Nintendo has revealed a bunch of offers in the US for this year's Black Friday in a hope to boost its sales ahead of the holiday season.
The headline here is a Switch 2 hardware bundle, which contains the console, a digital copy of Mario Kart World , and a 3-month individual membership to Nintendo Switch Online. Priced at $499.99 , this effectively wipes out the $50 price hike we saw earlier this year. This discount will be applicable from 22nd November to 5th December .
From 22nd November to 29th November , you can also bag $20 off the suggested retail price of select first-party games, including Donkey Kong Bananza and Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2 .
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
All of these offers will be available at Nintendo New York and Nintendo San Fransisco alongside select retailers. A Black Friday eShop sale will also kick off from 19th November, so keep an eye on Nintendo Life for our recommendations when the time comes.
Nintendo recently confirmed that the Switch 2 has surpassed 26 million console sales , despite a drop of around 37% year-on-year. The recent launch of Ocarina of Time will no doubt boost console sales nicely, as the game itself has already sold over 5 million copies .

articles.title_orig: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:

After being moored along Ireland’s boggy River Shannon estuary this week, the 120-metre-long (400-foot-long) cargo ship Karin set sail for Russia.
The vessel was laden with a bulk cargo of white powder that can be forged into weapons which are vital to Moscow’s war on Ukraine .
Alumina, a key ingredient in aluminium, goes into products from toothpaste and lipstick to missiles and drones.
A Russian-owned plant in southern Ireland operates as Europe’s biggest alumina refinery, regularly sending shiploads of the substance directly to St Petersburg and other Russian ports.
Almost five years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, alumina has escaped European sanctions intended to hobble Russia’s economy . That leaves the refinery in Aughinish free to send its product to Russia, where experts say some ends up in weapons.
“The material is clearly ending up in military supplies," said Irish politician Ivana Bacik, who leads the opposition Labour Party.
“It would be unthinkable for Ireland to be contributing, even in that indirect way, to Putin’s war machine.”
Ireland faces mounting calls to halt the shipments as dozens of European leaders gather in Dublin this week to discuss support for Ukraine. A summit of the 47-nation European Political Community on Thursday is being followed by a meeting of European Union leaders.
Irish government minister Niall Collins said that "there’s absolutely no evidence" the material is ending up in military supply chains, though the government has declined to publish the findings of its investigation into the alumina shipments.
Aughinish Alumina said in a statement its product “has no connection to the Russian military supply chain” and that it hired an independent company to provide monthly audits to Irish authorities for “enhanced traceability.”
Alumina is a chemical compound refined from bauxite, a red ore mined primarily in Guinea, Australia and China. The chalky white substance can be smelted into aluminum, which is then forged with other, rarer elements to make strong, heat-resistant and flexible alloys used in missiles and aircraft; aluminum is also used in the manufacture of rocket fuel and explosives.
The Aughinish plant in County Limerick was built in the 1970s and bought in 2007 by Rusal, a Russian aluminum producer. The company was founded, and is still part-owned, by Oleg Deripaska, a sanctioned oligarch with ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rusal makes virtually all of Russia's aluminum, according to the US and Australian governments.
While many cargo ships leave Aughinish bound for Europe and beyond, a steady stream of them heads straight to the port of St. Petersburg, according to data from MarineTraffic.
The activist group Alumina 22, which is lobbying to sanction the trade in alumina to Russia, estimated that between March and October some 491,307 metric tons of alumina from Ireland was shipped to Russia.
These shipments have grown in importance. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, two alumina factories – one in Australia, the other in Ukraine – stopped exporting to Russia, crimping its supplies by about 40 per cent, according to a 2026 report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine, or ESCU.
Roughly 17 per cent of Rusal's alumina supply now comes from Ireland, according to ESCU.
An investigation by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Irish Times , published earlier this year, found that alumina from Aughinish is smelted in Russia into aluminum, with some of it sold to a metals trading company that supplies Russian defense contractors.
“Virtually everything that comes from Rusal is with a high probability ending up in the hands of Russian military enterprises,” said Olena Yurchenko, director of analytics, research and investigations at the ESCU.
Standing next to Irish President Micheál Martin in Dublin in June, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said: “Unfortunately, there are companies in Europe that are owned or effectively controlled by Russia and its sanctioned oligarchs. They keep supplying the aggressor with essential materials, even now.”
Mr Martin acknowledged that “we do not want to be in a position where material emanating from a plant in Ireland goes to support the Russian war machine.”
Ireland has not found evidence that is happening — but also no proof it is not, said Enterprise Minister Peter Burke, who is in charge of the country's sanctions enforcement. He said in July it had been impossible to prove Rusal’s assertion that alumina from Ireland is only used to make aluminum for export from Russia.
The Irish government has not published its findings, but it handed them to the European Commission, which drafts EU sanctions packages.
EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan said there is little doubt that “the alumina goes to smelters in Russia who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex”.
“I’ve read the government report. Personally, I think there’s no doubt the investigative journalists got it right,” he said in October in Dublin at a meeting organized by the Institute of International and European Affairs.
The European Parliament in July passed a non-binding motion calling for a ban on alumina exports to Russia. But alumina was not included in the EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia that month. The EU’s executive European Commission, which draws up sanctions packages, is now sounding out member nations about the Irish alumina exports. Sanctions must be agreed upon unanimously by the bloc's 27 countries.
A commission spokesperson said in July that the bloc’s sanctions policy was “a delicate balance” between thwarting Russia’s war effort and limiting “negative impacts” on EU member nations, “especially considering that alumina is a critical raw material”.
Supporters of the plant point to the hundreds of jobs it provides, and to its role as a key source of alumina for European countries. Keeping supply lines open is especially important because of the chokehold on cargo traffic through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Mr Collins, who represents County Limerick in Ireland's parliament, said Ireland has been "hugely resolute in our support for the Ukrainians, and Ukraine hasn’t provided any evidence that Aughinish is doing anything adverse”.
Opposition politicians remain skeptical. Ms Bacik's left-of-center Labour Party supports a temporary nationalisation of the refinery, similar to when Ireland seized banks in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. She says the refinery can ban exports to Russia and find other eager customers in Europe.
“We need to see much stronger action being taken on this from other EU countries if the Irish government isn’t willing to do the right thing here,” she said.
In Foynes, the wind-swept port town beside the plant, many work at Aughinish or know someone who does. But some locals have mixed feelings.
“It's too big a business for them to close it down,” said retired docker Joe Hanlon. “Too much employment for the government to get involved.”
But he said “of course they should”, if Ireland wants “to stop the war on Ukraine”.
